paper: Gabaix & Koijen - In Search of the Origins of Financial Fluctuations: The Inelastic Markets Hypothesis
year: 2021 (NBER WP; SSRN metadata shows a Feb-2023 revision I could not reach - see notes)
version read: NBER w28967 PDF as currently hosted (file ModDate 2021-06-23); this is the only version NBER's own site links to, no rev1/rev2 present
quantity: AGGREGATE MARKET multiplier M (=1/aggregate demand elasticity), US equities
estimate: Headline M~5 per $1 of net flow. Benchmark GIV (Table 2, Flow-of-Funds sectors): M=7.1 (SE 1.9) with 1 principal component; M=5.3 (SE 1.10) with 2 PCs; implied aggregate elasticity zeta=0.13-0.17
range: Author-stated range $3-$8 per $1 across specifications; benchmark GIV point estimates 5.3-7.1
sample: US Flow of Funds, 12 continuously-held equity sectors, quarterly 1993Q1-2018Q4 (N=104); robustness with FactSet 13F and Morningstar mutual-fund flows, Jan1993-Dec2019
identification: Granular Instrumental Variables (GIV): size-weighted sum of sector-level idiosyncratic demand shocks (extracted via factor model on holdings changes) instruments the aggregate price change
critique: Self-stated: postpones what determines flows in the first place to future work (scope limitation, not a magnitude critique). External, from later papers I read at source: van Binsbergen-David-Opp (2026) show the paper's 'frictionless benchmark' macro-elasticity of 20 rests on an indeterminate equity/human-wealth allocation choice and 'can justify any value between -inf and +inf'; Hahn-He-Liao-Zhou (2026) replicate the exact design and find the original (FIV) estimator flips sign (-7.1) on a 6-sector subsample, though their corrected GIV estimator instead confirms/exceeds the headline (8.7-9.4) on that same subsample

paper: Haddad, Huebner & Loualiche - How Competitive is the Stock Market? Theory, Evidence from Portfolios, and Implications for the Rise of Passive Investing
version read: Author-hosted PDF (loualiche.com); content matches the AER-published framework (strategic-response/reflection model)
quantity: SINGLE-STOCK (cross-sectional) demand elasticity and its strategic-complementarity response to the aggregate elasticity of other investors
estimate: Strategic-response coefficient ~ -3 (a 1-unit rise in the market-wide aggregate elasticity for a stock lowers an individual investor's own elasticity by 3 units, i.e. 2/3 of a direct shock is offset). Average aggregate stock-level elasticity Eagg=0.438 (fixed-elasticity variant 0.39) -> implied single-stock multiplier ~2.3. A 32-percentage-point fall in active share over 20 years is estimated to make individual-stock demand 11% more inelastic
range: Eagg interquartile range 0.386 (25th pct) to 0.512 (75th pct) across stocks/dates
identification: Koijen-Yogo(2019)-style demand-system IV using variation in each institution's investment universe/AUM, plus a newly constructed instrument to identify the strategic-reaction (reflection) parameter separately from the direct elasticity
critique: Self-stated: assumes one constant strategic-response coefficient (chi) shared by all investors (functional-form restriction), tested but not fully relaxed. Paper explicitly frames itself as the single-stock analogue of, and contrast to, Gabaix-Koijen's aggregate-market estimate - it does not itself estimate the aggregate multiplier

paper: Chinco & Sammon - The Passive-Ownership Share Is Double What You Think It Is
version read: Author-hosted PDF (alexchinco.com / HBS mirror), matches JFE 2024 published version
quantity: (a) Passive ownership share of the US stock market (a measurement input, not an elasticity/multiplier). (b) SINGLE-STOCK price multiplier from index-reconstitution events, measured at varying horizons
estimate: (a) Overall passive ownership = 33.5% of US stock market cap in 2021, vs. ICI's commonly-cited 16% (i.e. ~2x). (b) At the shortest window (reconstitution day only): elasticity ~-39.2 (implied multiplier ~0.03, market looks 'too elastic'). At the longest window (full quarter before reconstitution): elasticity ~-1.1 (implied multiplier ~0.91), matching the ~1 micro-multiplier literature consensus
range: (a) 33.5% (38.5% if $2.25t of unmeasured direct indexing is added). (b) Across 6 indices, full-quarter-horizon elasticities range -0.7 to -3.3 (vs -0.6 to -88 at the reconstitution-day-only horizon)
sample: CRSP, US index reconstitutions (Russell 1000/2000, S&P500/MidCap400, Nasdaq100), 2000-2021
identification: (a) Abnormal reconstitution-day trading VOLUME (not returns) around index adds/deletes, cross-checked against known index-fund AUM. (b) Direct-addition natural experiment (a stock migrating between two adjacent indices has an offsetting buyer/seller base), price impact measured over trading windows from 1 to 60 days before reconstitution
critique: Self-stated central point: prior single-stock elasticity estimates using only reconstitution-day price/volume (e.g. Wurgler & Zhuravskaya 2002, range -11.72 to -1.00) are biased toward looking 'too elastic' because passive trades are prescheduled and priced in days/weeks before execution; excludes index deletions as confounded by bankruptcy/M&A

paper: Jiang, Vayanos & Zheng - Passive Investing and the Rise of Mega-Firms
year: 2025 (RFS 38(12):3461-, published); LSE-hosted draft dated 2025-06-19; first circulated as NBER w28253 (2020)
version read: personal.lse.ac.uk/vayanos hosted PDF, dated 19 June 2025 (post-NBER, matches RFS-published framing)
quantity: FACTOR/SIZE-LEVEL: differential sensitivity of large-cap ('mega-firm') stock returns to passive (S&P500 index-fund) flow. Not a single aggregate-market dollar multiplier - the paper's claim is that pure active-to-passive SWITCHING (zero net new money) can still raise the aggregate market via this size channel
estimate: A 1-standard-deviation rise in standardized quarterly S&P500 passive flow raises the top-50 (by size) portfolio's quarterly excess return by 0.53pp (range 0.53-0.56pp across specs); sensitivity rises monotonically with concentration: +0.145pp (top200) to +0.687pp (top10) per 1-SD flow. Cumulated over the 99-quarter sample, a hypothetical always-top-50 firm is implied to have outperformed the index by ~29% purely from the rise in indexing
range: 0.145pp (top-200 portfolio) to 0.687pp (top-10 portfolio) per 1-SD flow shock; theory-calibration illustrations (distinct from the empirical estimate) show pure active-to-passive switching raising the aggregate market by 0.09%-3.6% in various scenarios
sample: CRSP + S&P500 index-fund/ETF/mutual-fund holdings (CRSP), quarterly, ~1996-2020 (99 quarters)
identification: OLS time-series regression of size-sorted portfolio excess returns on realized (standardized) S&P500 passive fund flow, controlling for contemporaneous/lagged S&P500 return and VIX. No instrument is used for flow/return endogeneity in this main test; the causal reading rests on the theoretical model plus the monotonic size pattern, which is harder to explain via reverse causality alone
critique: No explicit IV for the core empirical test (unlike GK/Haddad et al./Pavlova-Sikorskaya), a fair identification caveat I infer from the absence of any instrument/endogeneity discussion around the main regressions. The paper's headline contribution is conceptual/compositional (why the aggregate market can rise from switching alone), not a new re-estimate of the net-flow multiplier

paper: van der Beck - On the Estimation of Demand-Based Asset Pricing Models (Ch.1 of PhD thesis 'Demand-based Asset Pricing: Theory, Estimation and Applications')
version read: EPFL Infoscience thesis PDF, Chapter 1 (pp.1-33 of thesis)
quantity: SINGLE-STOCK/institutional demand elasticity, re-estimated from trades (holdings changes) rather than holdings levels as in Koijen & Yogo (2019, 'KY')
estimate: AUM-weighted average institutional elasticity ~0.7 (changes + flow-instrument) vs. KY(2019)'s constrained levels-based estimate, ~4x smaller in this magnitude (so multiplier roughly 4x lower than KY's constrained estimate would imply)
range: '4 times larger' than KY(2019) is the paper's own headline ratio; KY(2019) diagonal multiplier-matrix elements elsewhere cited (by van der Beck and others) as 2-4
sample: US institutional 13F holdings (Thomson/Refinitiv Institutional Holdings), quarterly, 2000-2021
identification: Estimation-in-changes (trades, not levels) instrumented by flow-induced mutual-fund demand shocks, orthogonalized against fund-specific characteristics to strip fundamental information; exogeneity supported by price-pressure reverting after ~1.5 years
critique: Self-stated: identifies an omitted-variable bias in the standard KY(2019) cross-sectional-LEVELS approach (unobserved static portfolio mandates correlate with price levels, biasing elasticities toward zero / multipliers too large); also notes KY(2019)'s unconstrained levels estimates are frequently upward-sloping (economically implausible), which is why KY impose an artificial positivity constraint

paper: van der Beck - Flow-Driven ESG Returns (Ch.2 of the same PhD thesis)
quantity: FACTOR/BASKET-LEVEL price multiplier for a green/ESG stock basket vs. the market
estimate: Structural ESG multiplier ~1.11 (1% green-basket demand shock -> 1.11% price change); cross-sectional reduced-form estimate 1.17 (close to structural); every $1 flowing from the market portfolio into the representative ESG portfolio raises the aggregate value of green stocks by $0.4; flow-driven price pressure is estimated to explain virtually all of the ESG portfolio's realized outperformance (counterfactual without ESG flows: annualized 5-factor alpha of -0.3% instead of the actual positive alpha)
range: 0.87 to 1.69 across identification approaches (structural model / cross-sectional regression / Vanguard-4Good index-inclusion event study)
sample: US institutional 13F + mutual-fund holdings, 2010-2021; ESG-fund return sample 2016-2021 (551 identified ESG mutual funds)
identification: Same trades+flow-instrument estimator as Ch.1, applied to a green-vs-market demand system; robustness check re-instruments using changes in Pavlova & Sikorskaya's Benchmarking Intensity as an alternative, supply-side instrument
critique: Self-addresses the 'Wardlaw (2020) critique' of flow-induced-trade instruments, claiming immunity by construction (self-stated, not independently re-derived by me here). This is a factor/basket-level estimate, not the aggregate US equity multiplier

year: 2022 (NBER WP w30688, Nov 2022); published as 'Market-Wide Predictable Price Pressure', AER 2025, 115(9):3171-3213
quantity: AGGREGATE MARKET-level price multiplier, identified from predictable (pre-announced) dividend-reinvestment flows
estimate: Market-level price multiplier of 1.5 to 2.3 per $1 (preferred estimate, scaling by investor-group reinvestment rates); simple back-of-envelope lower bound of 0.67 assuming 100% reinvestment
sample: CRSP US equities, 1926-2018 (main dividend/reinvestment sample); international cross-check 1986-2017; sub-tests on FOMC/macro announcement windows 1988-2019 and 1994-2019
identification: Scheduled/pre-announced timing of dividend payments and reinvestment as a source of uninformed, non-fundamental demand shocks; effect scaled to a market-wide multiplier using estimated reinvestment rates by investor type (retail, mutual fund, institutional)
critique: Self-stated, direct comparison at source: 'somewhat lower than that in Gabaix and Koijen (2021), showing... the multiplier estimated may be sensitive to methodology and which flows are used for estimation.' Also flags their own puzzle: because the dividend flow is announced weeks in advance, its large price effect at execution is 'puzzlingly large' under standard models (including Gabaix-Koijen's), which predict most of the price move should occur at announcement, not execution

paper: Parker, Schoar & Sun - Retail Financial Innovation and Stock Market Dynamics: The Case of Target Date Funds
year: 2021 (NBER w28028, revised Aug 2021); published Journal of Finance 2023, 78(5):2673-2723
quantity: SINGLE-STOCK-level demand elasticity for stocks with high indirect ownership by target-date/balanced funds ('TDBFs'), from contrarian rebalancing flows. (A separate aggregate-market figure is an illustrative calibration using Gabaix-Koijen's own M=5, not a new estimate.)
estimate: Demand elasticity -0.3 -> 'an additional dollar of [TDBF] demand ... the price ... rises by three dollars' (implied single-stock multiplier ~3). Illustrative calibration: at TDBFs' current ~4% of US equity market, contrarian rebalancing dampens a 10-percentage-point equity-minus-bond return gap to 9.4pp (using GK's M=5); would dampen it to 7pp if TDBF equity share grew to 20%
range: Authors flag their point estimate (multiplier ~3) as much higher than typical single-stock index-inclusion estimates (elasticity ~-1, multiplier ~1; e.g. Shleifer 1986, Chang-Hong-Liskovich 2015)
sample: US mutual funds/TDFs; monthly individual stock returns 2010-2018; TDF asset data 2000-2019
identification: TDF glide-path-implied contrarian rebalancing demand (mechanical function of the equity-vs-bond return gap and fund mandate) as an instrument for indirect institutional demand, scaled by each stock's estimated indirect TDF/balanced-fund ownership
critique: Self-stated: authors interrogate why their single-stock estimate is so much larger than the idiosyncratic index-inclusion literature and conclude the likely reason is that arbitrage capital does not trade against TDF flows (unlike one-off idiosyncratic events), because doing so requires bearing undiversifiable systematic risk - i.e. systematic demand shocks plausibly command a structurally larger multiplier than idiosyncratic ones

year: 2022 (WP dated 7 March 2022); published Review of Financial Studies 2023, 36(3):859-903
quantity: SINGLE-STOCK-level price impact / demand elasticity of benchmarked institutional investors
estimate: Price impact (multiplier) = 1.47 per $1 (2SLS; essentially identical with 1 or 2 instruments). Implied household/residual-investor demand elasticity ~2.26. Using mutual-fund/ETF ownership alone instead of all institutional ownership raises the estimate to ~2.6, which the authors flag as attributing too much impact to funds specifically
range: 1.47 (baseline, preferred) to 2.6 (fund-only alternative, authors' own caveat); compare to Koijen & Yogo (2019) institution-level range of 2-4 cited by the authors as consistent
sample: US 13F institutional holdings + CRSP returns, 1998-2018; Russell 1000/2000 cutoff, bandwidth of 300 stocks around the cutoff (N=12,862 stock-year observations)
identification: Change in Benchmarking Intensity (BMI - a stock's cumulative weight across all benchmarks it belongs to, asset-weighted) instruments for the change in institutional ownership, exploiting the Russell 1000/2000 index-assignment discontinuity; over-identified with a second instrument (index-membership dummy), Hansen J-test does not reject (p=0.19)
critique: Self-stated upper-bound caveat: anticipatory arbitrage trading ahead of the (May-determined, predictable) Russell reassignment is not fully captured in their measurement window, so 'our baseline estimate of elasticity is an upper bound' (true elasticity may be lower / multiplier higher). This is a single-stock, local-to-cutoff estimate, not an aggregate-market one

paper: Li & Lin - Price Multipliers are Larger at More Aggregate Levels
version read: Rutgers-hosted PDF mirror (business.rutgers.edu); also circulated as SSRN 4038664, not accessed directly
quantity: Price multiplier estimated simultaneously at three levels of aggregation (idiosyncratic stock / granular style / coarse style) with one unified demand instrument; a secondary diagnostic exercise attempts literal market-level (aggregate) estimation
estimate: Multiplier rises with aggregation: 1.73 (idiosyncratic stock) -> 3.12 (granular style) -> 6.98 (coarse style); differences are statistically significant. A naive extension of the same instrument to the literal whole market gives an implausible 25.7-32.9, which the authors attribute to omitted-variable bias from correlated S&P futures order flow (estimated bias ~27.9 per $1, 95% CI [11.5, 44.2]); they explicitly conclude 'our measure should not be used to estimate market-level price multipliers'
range: 1.73-6.98 across the three validated aggregation levels; [C-076] the paper reports NO bias-corrected market-level figure; it concludes the measure should not be used for market-level multipliers (naive ~32.85, estimated bias ~27.9, roughly ~5) is coincidentally close to Gabaix-Koijen's own aggregate estimate
sample: US equities, weekly Lee-Ready signed order-flow imbalance (TAQ-based), 1993-2022
identification: Demand decomposed into coarse-style / granular-style / idiosyncratic components via size and book-to-market sorts (and, as a robustness check, a data-driven alternative), each regressed on contemporaneous stock returns; robust across sub-periods within 1993-2022
critique: Self-stated: an explicit methodological critique of naively extending microstructure order-flow measures to the aggregate/market level (severe omitted-variable bias from correlated index-futures flow). Their positive finding (multipliers rise with aggregation) favors risk-averse-liquidity-provider explanations over information-based ones for why single-stock and aggregate multipliers differ so much

paper: van Binsbergen, David & Opp - How (Not) to Identify Demand Elasticities in Dynamic Asset Markets
version read: Duke Fuqua conference-hosted PDF, dated 27 March 2026
quantity: METHODOLOGICAL/THEORETICAL: necessary conditions for valid identification of demand elasticities in dynamic (multi-period) asset markets; not a new large-sample empirical aggregate-multiplier estimate
estimate: Illustrative recalibration of Gabaix-Koijen's 'frictionless benchmark': shifter-elasticity eta~0.28 (pseudo-multiplier~2.34) vs. GK's claimed frictionless macro-elasticity of 20, which the authors show depends on an indeterminate equity/human-wealth allocation assumption that 'can justify any value between -infinity and +infinity'. Separately show a large fraction of KY(2019)-style elasticity estimates turn negative once an ad hoc positivity constraint is relaxed
range: Not applicable - a theoretical bias characterization, not a new field point estimate for the actual US aggregate multiplier
sample: Not applicable (theoretical paper; no new panel/time-series estimation of the aggregate multiplier itself)
identification: Formal dynamic general-equilibrium argument that commonly used instruments violate the exclusion restriction whenever the instrumented price shift is persistent or predictable, in which case what is identified is a shock-process-specific 'shifter-process elasticity', not the structural demand elasticity
critique: This paper IS itself the critique: names Gabaix & Koijen (2023) and Koijen & Yogo (2019, 2021) directly and argues published elasticity estimates in this literature 'are off by orders of magnitude, or even have the wrong sign'; also argues the theoretical 'frictionless benchmark' (macro elasticity ~10-20) used to frame markets as puzzlingly inelastic is itself not well identified

paper: Hahn, He, Liao & Zhou - Granular Instrumental Variables: Estimation and Inference
year: 2026 (arXiv v1, posted 12 June 2026; draft dated 15 June 2026)
quantity: AGGREGATE US equity market multiplier, re-estimated on Gabaix-Koijen's exact sample/design using a new fixed-n GIV estimator with formal specification testing
estimate: 12-sector panel: GIV=5.05 (1993Q1-2018Q4) / 4.46 (extended 1988Q4-2025Q4) - but the overidentification (J) test REJECTS this specification (p<0.001) in both samples. 6-sector 'granular core' (>97% of equity holdings; J-test does NOT reject, p=0.82/0.59): GIV=8.70 (1993-2018) / 9.42 (1988-2025). The ORIGINAL Gabaix-Koijen-style (FIV) estimator turns NEGATIVE on that same 6-sector data (-7.13, -2.15) - a robustness failure their new GIV corrects
range: 4.46-9.42 depending on sector grouping; the authors' own valid (non-rejected) specification favors the higher end (8.7-9.4). Uninstrumented OLS (upward-biased benchmark) gives 5.42-11.42
sample: US Financial Accounts (Flow of Funds) Table L.224, 12 continuously-observed equity-holding sectors; benchmark 1993Q1-2018Q4 (T=104, identical to Gabaix-Koijen's own sample) and an extended sample 1988Q4-2025Q4 (T=149)
identification: New GIV moment-based estimator built from the orthogonal complement of the (possibly unknown) factor-loading space, valid without requiring the number of sectors to grow; includes a formal overidentification (Hansen J) test not available in the original GK framework
critique: Shows GK's original (FIV) estimator is fragile to sector grouping (sign flip under the 6-sector core). Shows the full 12-sector homogeneous-elasticity specification - the one that reproduces GK's own ~5 - is formally REJECTED by their own overidentification test, implying elasticities likely differ materially across sectors (consistent with Qian, below). Their own preferred, test-passing estimate (8.7-9.4) is HIGHER than GK's headline ~5, not lower

quantity: AGGREGATE US equity elasticity re-estimated allowing fully unrestricted cross-sector heterogeneity (RGIV estimator), on the identical Gabaix-Koijen sample
estimate: Size-weighted aggregate elasticity = -0.05 (implied multiplier ~20 per $1 - MORE inelastic/larger multiplier than Gabaix-Koijen's own ~5). Block-level heterogeneity: Retirement & Insurance -0.2 (multiplier ~5); Real Domestic -0.08 (multiplier ~12.5); Foreign ~0 (multiplier very large/near-undefined); Intermediaries & Funds +0.09 (upward-sloping demand - not economically a 'multiplier' at all for that block). Between-block homogeneity is formally rejected
range: Block elasticities range from +0.09 (perverse/upward-sloping) to about -0.2, i.e. implied block multipliers range from economically invalid (negative) to >20
sample: Identical to Gabaix-Koijen: US Flow of Funds, 12 sectors, quarterly 1993Q1-2018Q4
identification: RGIV - a GMM-based generalization of GIV that drops GK's shock-variance and size-skewness conditions and leaves cross-sector heterogeneity fully unrestricted (rather than tying it to observables as GK's own extensions do)
critique: Does not reject the inelastic-markets hypothesis - if anything implies an even larger size-weighted multiplier than GK - but formally REJECTS the single-homogeneous-elasticity assumption underlying GK's benchmark specification, and shows standard GIV confidence intervals 'can undercover' (be overconfident) under realistic heterogeneity and unknown shock variances
